title: "Wait! Why is everyone connected to mine?!”: Contextualizing Rule Breaking as a Design Affordance
citation: Naomi G. Lau, Christina Stiso, Selena Steinberg, Mengxi Zhou, Chris Cruz-Gonzalez, Merijke Coenraad, Joshua Danish (2026). "Wait! Why is everyone connected to mine?!”: Contextualizing Rule Breaking as a Design Affordance. Proceedings of ICLS 2026.
abstract: This paper looks at a network visualization software and a middle school activity to explore how design affordances, and youth agency intersect in learning. Despite equitable design intentions through limiting students to three connections in the network, some students exceeded that rule, producing larger nodes that drew attention to rule -breaking. Findings show how technical affordances simultaneously intersect with rule breaking, and youth agency and expression, suggesting that even well -intentioned lesson designs can constrain youth agency and participation. By integrating literature on design justice and network visualization, these case studies reveal how data representations not only mediate participation, but also takes into consideration youth agency constraints. Youth agency emphasizes the importance of youth participation, and meaning making of the world around them. This study calls for justice - centered reflexive design that anticipates and honors student agency.

authors: Lau, N. G., Stiso, C., Steinberg, S., Zhou, M., Cruz-Gonzalez, C., Coenraad, M., & Danish, J.

title: (Mis)aligning dialogic practices and beliefs: Teacher change during video- based professional development
citation: Pengjin Wang, Liru Hu, Kexin Li, Gaowei Chen (2026). (Mis)aligning dialogic practices and beliefs: Teacher change during video- based professional development. Proceedings of ICLS 2026.
abstract: This case study investigates how teacher beliefs, practices, and perceptions of student ability jointly shape the trajectories of teacher change within a video- based professional development (PD) programme on dialogic teaching. Through a comparative analysis of two English language teachers who participated in five monthly PD cycles, we triangulated data from student surveys, teacher reflections, and post -PD interviews. Findings reveal that while both teachers attempted to use Academically Productive Talk moves, their underlying beliefs critically mediated the outcomes. The teacher with constructivist and evaluatist beliefs fostered a co -constructive classroom and achieved significant gains in student perceived discursive engagement. The teacher with transmissive and absolutist beliefs appropriated talk moves for recitation, with no significant student perceived impact. The study concludes that effective PD must move beyond transmitting tools to explicitly target and support the evolution of teacher beliefs, which act as the primary filter for pedagogical change.
notes: Non-digital or conceptual paper; can be verified via Tier 2.
authors: Wang, P., Hu, L., Li, K., & Chen, G.

title: (Re)constructing What Counts: The Politics and Possibilities of Teacher Noticing
citation: Karen Underwood, Ilana Horn (2026). (Re)constructing What Counts: The Politics and Possibilities of Teacher Noticing. Proceedings of ICLS 2026.
abstract: Teacher noticing, defined as teachers’ ability to attend to and interpret classroom events, constitutes a dominant construct supporting teacher preparation programs and professional development. This conceptual paper argues that noticing frameworks do not simply describe professional knowledge, but actively shape what counts as knowledge in teaching. Dominant cognitive and sociocultural approaches privilege analytical, observable, and individually located forms of knowing while overlooking the tacit, embodied, and r elational dimensions that teachers draw on within their practice, carrying political consequences for how teachers are supported. Building on emerging ecological and relational approaches, we argue that reimagining the construct opens possibilities for recognizing the full range of knowledge teachers draw on in their practice. Through an illustrative example with an experienced secondary mathematics teacher, Clark, we explore what becomes possible when research begins from teachers’ lived experience.
notes: Non-digital or conceptual paper; can be verified via Tier 2.
authors: Underwood, K. & Horn, I.

title: A CSCL Taxonomy Building Workshop
citation: Martin Greisel, Burcu Şener, Sebastian Simon, Conrad Borchers, Elham Tajik, Bahar Shahrokhian (2026). A CSCL Taxonomy Building Workshop. Proceedings of ISLS 2026.
abstract: This workshop aims at collaboratively developing a shared taxonomy for the Computer-Supported Collaborative Learning (CSCL) community that captures diverse epistemological, methodological and technological perspectives to help build a common ground for CSCL research. Through pre-workshop Delphi input, hands-on application, and iterative refinement, participants co-construct a framework to support clearer communication, cumulative knowledge building, and more transparent dissemination in CSCL proceedings and journals. The resulting taxonomy and follow-up activities aim to strengthen community identity, foster collaboration, and guide future CSCL research and publication practices. Organizers ● Martin Greisel: Assistant professor/postdoc at the University of Augsburg, focusing on regulation in collaborative learning, peer feedback, and teacher training. ● Burcu Şener: Lecturer at Middle East Technical University, PhD candidate at Bogazici University, focusing on collaborative problem solving, collaborative debugging, computational thinking. ● Sebastian Simon: Postdoctoral fellow at the University of Le Mans with a PhD in Computer Science. During his PhD, he focused on enhancing mobile and co-located Computer-Supported Collaborative Learning with Augmented Reality (AR). In his current Postdoc position, he investigates generative AI agents as collaborative entities in co-located CSCL settings. ● Conrad Borchers: PhD candidate at Carnegie Mellon University, researching data science and HCI applications to improve educational processes. ● Elham Tajik: PhD student at the University at Albany, she focuses on the transformative role of generative AI in education and HCI. ● Bahar Shahrokhian: PhD candidate at Arizona State University, researching multimodal learning analytics and collaboration in co-located learning environments. Intended audience and resources This half-day workshop is intended for all researchers and educators interested and engaged in CSCL, as well as its related domains, including but not limited to: educational psychologists, computer scientists and learning scientists. We particularly welcome researchers from all domains to contribute their vision of computer-supported collaborative learning, with a minimum of 8 to a maximum of 40 participants. We can manage up to 30 in-person and 10 online (Zoom) participants. Regarding resources, we only need a large seminar room with WiFi and a projector that enables group work through flexible tables (i.e., no lecture hall with fixed rows). In-person participants will be asked to bring their personal laptops. Description of the event Theme and goals In recent years, the field of Computer-Supported Collaborative Learning (CSCL) has continued to expand in scope, methods, and theoretical foundations. While this diversity reflects the richness and vitality of the field, it also creates challenges for integration and cumulative knowledge building. Researchers draw on a wide range of epistemological, methodological, and technological perspectives, and often work in parallel rather than in concert. This fragmentation can make it difficult to identify shared concerns, trace the development of ideas, or recognize complementarities among approaches. At the same time, the multiplicity of perspectives represents an invaluable resource. If systematically understood and connected, this multiplicity can foster deeper insights into learning processes and the design of collaborative technologies. Previous CSCL workshops have identified the need for a common language across the different domains that are present in the CSCL community. Common language p resents the first step to common ground, a concept that is key to the knowledge building in a scientific community, particularly in one that emphasizes the strength of co-existing paradigms, requiring awareness of semiotic and semantic differences (that may otherwise lead to issues like gatekeeping or siloed research, Kuhn, 1962). Particularly, the 2025 CSCL workshop participants have identified the need for community building in the CSCL field and the potential of a collaboratively created CSCL taxonomy as an artefact for building common ground. Consequently, this workshop has two goals: (1) community building and (2) taxonomy development. To build community, the workshop brings together members of the CSCL community to overcome fragmentation and to harness the richness of the field’s diversity. It will help strengthen a community identity by creating an awareness of what constitutes CSCL and foster a feeling of agency through a common activity centered around the community itself (Wise & Schwarz, 2017). The second goal is to develop a taxonomy for classifying future CSCL research, especially contributions to future conference proceedings and ijCSCL articles. This taxonomy aims to offer a shared framework that reflects the community’s pluralistic character while enabling more coherent navigation, communication, comparison, and synthesis of research. As a tangible outcome and lasting artefact, it aims to promote collaboration across paradigmatic differences in the future. In addition, the process of developing such a taxonomy itself constitutes an effort of community building, thereby also serving the first goal of the workshop. In summary, by collaboratively developing and validating such a taxonomy, supported by a broad proportion of the CSCL community, the workshop seeks to lay the foundation for a more connected and integrated future for CSCL research. Theoretical background and relevance to the field and conference CSCL is inherently multidisciplinary, integrating perspectives from at least the learning sciences, educational sciences, psychology, and computer science. This diversity enriches the field but also introduces substantial variation in researchers’ underlying epistemic stances. According to the AIR model (Chinn et al., 2014), such stances encompass differences in 3 ways. First, researchers have different aims—they seek to achieve different things with their work. Second, they hold different ideals—they disagree on what counts as valid knowledge and good evidence and the criteria by which success is evaluated. Third, they use different reliable processes—they favor different methods for how data is created and interpreted, that is, the methods considered most appropriate to reach their aims. While this pluralism fosters innovation and theoretical breadth, it also poses challenges for mutual understanding in our field. Researchers examining similar phenomena may struggle to find, understand, and interpret each other’s research contributions because they pursue different aims, evaluate knowledge by different criteria, and employ different methods. This is reflected, for example, in the co-existence of different major theoretical traditions (e.g., constructivist and sociocultural, cognitive/information‑processing), a focus on different mid-level theories or theory-driven pedagogical frameworks (e.g., knowledge building, cognitive load theory, theory of immersive collaborative learning) or interactional constructs (e.g., transactivity, socio‑cognitive conflict) and competence frameworks (e.g., collaborative problem‑solving skills), and different analytical and design methodologies (e.g., collaborative analytics or design-based research) (Brown, 1992; Dillenbourg, 1999; Graesser et al., 2018; Kirschner et al., 2018; Makransky & Petersen, 2023; Scardamalia & Bereiter, 2014; Vogel et al., 2023; Vygotsky, 1978; Wise et al., 2023). As a result, communication across perspectives can become fragmented, leading to disciplinary silos and limited knowledge integration within the CSCL community (Wise & Schwarz, 2017), thereby hindering the advancement of knowledge. To remedy fragmentation, a workshop at the CSCL 2025 conference aimed at developing a shared paradigm (see also section “Relationship to similar events conducted in the past” below). However, one main outcome, also advocated by a panel of senior CSCL scholars, was that attempting to unify the CSCL community under a single theoretical or methodological framework would weaken the field’s richness in diversity. Its multi- perspectivity is not a weakness to be corrected, but a strength that enables deeper and more comprehensive inquiry. As a result, the goal should be to bridge epistemic diversity to enable constructive dialogue rather than to simply erase different perspectives and epistemologies. A step toward bridging these differences is to establish a shared vocabulary that enables researchers to articulate their approaches in a comparable manner (Wise & Schwarz, 2017). When organized systematically, such a vocabulary can take the form of a taxonomy—a structured set of dimensions and descriptors that capture from which viewpoint researchers approach their investigation, which phenomenon they study, and how they study it. A CSCL taxonomy could thus provide a common reference point for describing research aims,

title: A Case Study on the Effect of TAs’ Awareness of Pre-class Report Submissions on Scaffolding in Small-group Discussions
citation: Nozomi Fujikawa, Sanii Mizuno, Shintaro Uchiyama (2026). A Case Study on the Effect of TAs’ Awareness of Pre-class Report Submissions on Scaffolding in Small-group Discussions. Proceedings of CSCL 2026.
abstract: In recent years, Teaching Assistants (TAs) have been expected to play a key role in facilitating small-group discussions. However, prior studies have shown that TAs often struggle to provide appropriate interventions, frequently offering task- related explanations without first diagnosing students’ understanding. This study examined whether awareness of students’ pre- class report submissions supported TAs’ diagnostic scaffolding during small-group discussions. A 100-minute class session was video -recorded, and all TA utterances were transcribed and analyzed based on the framework of the Model of Contingent Teaching (MCT), focusing on the diagnostic and intervention phases. The results suggest that although both TAs were aware of students’ pre-class report submissions, only one TA engaged in diagnostic questioning to assess students’ understanding before intervening, whereas the other tended to respond with empathic support without diagnosis. This study extends the MCT to TA-supported learning environments by emphasizing the importance of recognizing pre-class reports and highlighting the interpretive processes that mediate between information awareness and adaptive intervention.

title: A Common Language for Infrastucturing Maker Education: Mapping Stakeholder Challenges and Opportunities using a Five-Dimensional Framework
citation: Hila Langer, Yuval Segev, Shiri Kashi, Yotam Hod (2026). A Common Language for Infrastucturing Maker Education: Mapping Stakeholder Challenges and Opportunities using a Five-Dimensional Framework. Proceedings of ICLS 2026.
abstract: The promise of maker education is frequently constrained by entrenched educational infrastructures. Efforts to create sustainable change, a process known as infrastructuring, require a deep and shared understanding of systemic challenges and opportunities . However, discourse among stakeholders can be diffuse, hindering collective action. To address this, we propose a five -dimensional analytic framework —epistemological, pedagogical, social, material-technological, and organizational —as a tool for mapping the landscape of maker education. We convened a conference of diverse stakeholders and analyzed their roundtable discussions about the future of maker education. Preliminary findings reveal that stakeholders’ articulations of core problems and potential solutions align with the five dimensions of our framework, even without its explicit introduction. This suggests the framework's potential as a tool to help communities surface, structure, and formalize their grounded knowledge, fostering a common language vital for intentional infrastructuring work.

title: A Community-Engaged Curriculum Design Model for Culturally-Responsive Tech Consulting
citation: Annie Zhou, Kristin Seefeldt, Julie Hui, Christie Baer, Lutalo Sanifu, Tawanna R. Dillahunt (2026). A Community-Engaged Curriculum Design Model for Culturally-Responsive Tech Consulting. Proceedings of ICLS 2026.
abstract: Minority small businesses operating in resource -constrained areas are actively building their digital capacity while facing significant barriers that existing digital services fail to address. We designed and implemented the Community Tech Consultants (CTC s) program to address this gap by offering accessible and effective digital support grounded in a deep understanding of these businesses’ realities, challenges, and needs. To deepen community partnerships and meaningfully engage university students, this study aims to develop a community-engaged curriculum that prepares students for culturally responsive tech consulting with these businesses, and that can be adapted across diverse cultural and community contexts. Through design -based research and co -design with community partners, we propose a community-engaged curriculum design model with five interrelated elements: co -design and co-instruction, authentic learning, adaptive scaffolding, iteration, and adaptability. We extend the discourse on cultural responsiveness in community- engaged learning and underscore the value of co-design between the community and the university.

title: A Design Space for Dialogic Assessment in CSCL
citation: Rolf Steier, Magnus Hontvedt, Jacob Davidsen, Charlotte Beal, Morten Oddvik, Marit Solem (2026). A Design Space for Dialogic Assessment in CSCL. Proceedings of CSCL 2026.
abstract: Dialogic assessment remains remarkably unexplored as a research and design setting in CSCL. We address this gap by developing a design space to support future partnership-based work in our field. Our design space reflects a 1.5- year investigation of dialogic assessment practices and perspectives conducted through literature review work, focus group interviews with practitioners, formal and informal discussions with colleagues and prototype development work with technology designers. First, we frame the design space concept before arguing for the relevance of dialogic assessment as a potential CSCL activity. Then, we present our design space through a cumulative distillation of four relevant perspectives and seven design dimensions. Finally, we conclude by laying out an agenda reflecting how this design space can inform future work and prompt innovative assessment practices.

title: A Double-Edged Sword: Navigating Hope and Concern in Teachers’ Adoption of AI Image Generation Tools
citation: Jihyun Rho, Younsun Choi, Shamya Karumbaiah (2026). A Double-Edged Sword: Navigating Hope and Concern in Teachers’ Adoption of AI Image Generation Tools. Proceedings of ICLS 2026.
abstract: Generative AI is rapidly entering classrooms, offering both opportunities and challenges for K-12 education. While text-based models have received extensive attention, the educational implications of AI image generation tools remain largely unexplored. Thi s study examines how K -12 teachers perceive the benefits, risks, and pedagogical uses of such tools. We conducted semi-structured interviews with six U.S. teachers across diverse grade levels and subject areas, combining discussion of current practices with a hands -on prompt-engineering activity. Thematic analysis revealed a persistent tension between teachers’ enthusiasm for efficiency, customization, and creativity, and their deep ethical concerns about bias, stereotypes, and cultural representation. Teachers emphasized the need for knowledge beyond operational skills, including critical understanding of AI’s underlying logic and limitations. Findings point to a pedagogical shift from using generative AI merely for content production toward leveraging it as a tool for fostering critical inquiry, with implications for teacher professional development and equitable learning design.
notes: General instructional setting; can be verified via Tier 2.

title: A First Grader Making Sense of Graphs: A Knowledge-in-Pieces Account of Functional Thinking
citation: Mathías A. López, Susanne Strachota, Johyeon Chang, Bárbara M. Brizuela, Maria Blanton, Angela (2026). A First Grader Making Sense of Graphs: A Knowledge-in-Pieces Account of Functional Thinking. Proceedings of ICLS 2026.
abstract: We present the case of Lucca (pseudonym), a six -year-old who participated in three interviews before, during, and after a classroom teaching experiment on function graphs. We analyzed his reasoning by identifying the resources he drew on: seeds of algebraic thinking and resources tied to the graph. Lucca’s functional thinking can be understood through the lens of Knowledge in Pieces: recursive and functional reasoning was supported by his coordination of resources. As his functional thinking developed, the seeds he used remained consistent, but the resources tied to the graph he coordinated were different.

title: A Latent Profile Analysis of Math Self-Efficacy and Anxiety in Game-Based Learning
citation: Alireza (Sina) Zandi, Leyla Karami Isheqlou, Jody Clarke-Midura (2026). A Latent Profile Analysis of Math Self-Efficacy and Anxiety in Game-Based Learning. Proceedings of ICLS 2026.
abstract: This study investigated how math anxiety and self- efficacy shape students’ algebra learning in From Here to There! (FH2T), a digital game for algebraic reasoning. Data from 607 seventh graders were analyzed using Latent Profile Analysis, identifying five p rofiles representing unique combinations of math performance, worry, and emotional reaction. Grounded in Self -Efficacy Theory, the findings show how belief in ability shapes students’ emotional and cognitive experiences in digital learning.

title: A Mixed-Method Analysis of Facilitator Sensemaking around Social-Emotional Learning in a Refugee Summer Program
citation: Hiba Khatib, Sarah Priscilla Lee (2026). A Mixed-Method Analysis of Facilitator Sensemaking around Social-Emotional Learning in a Refugee Summer Program. Proceedings of ICLS 2026.
abstract: This study utilizes a mixed -methods approach to analyze facilitator sensemaking around social-emotional learning (SEL). Using Latent Dirichlet Allocation (topic modeling) and grounded theory coding, we analyze two corpora of SEL literature to identify key topics that comprise dominant and critical SEL frameworks. Our findings reveal that while dominant SEL frameworks emphasize institutional language, critical SEL frameworks better reflect the complex cultural negotiations that facilitators navigate in their practice. Qualitative analysis of facilitator interviews validates these computational findings, illustrating how facilitators draw on their own cultural backgrounds as underscored in critical approaches to SEL. This study supports the need for SEL frameworks that can accommodate multiple ways of understanding social and emotional development in culturally diverse contexts.

title: A Multimodal Study of Emotion Regulation in Student Dyads During Computational Model Building
citation: Ashwin T S, Srigowri Mayasandra Prasanna, Joyce Fonteles, Gautam Biswas (2026). A Multimodal Study of Emotion Regulation in Student Dyads During Computational Model Building. Proceedings of CSCL 2026.
abstract: Collaborative problem solving (CPS) requires coordination of cognition and affect in complex, open-ended tasks. This study examines how pairs of high school students regulate learner-centered emotions (engagement, confusion, frustration, boredom, and delight ) while constructing computational models in a STEM+C context. Extending Gross’s (2015) process model to the group level, we analyze temporal dynamics of synchronized and unsynchronized emotional states during CPS. Multimodal data from six dyads (video, audio, system logs) were coded for CPS activities (e.g., information sharing, consensus building) and emotion transitions. Emotional alignment predominated, yet brief misalignments (especially between engagement and confusion) were frequent and often precipitated interpersonal regulation. Temporal analysis identified two dominant pathways: (1) transitions from misalignment to alignment that restore shared engagement, and (2) transitions between aligned states that shift partners from shared confusion to engagement. These pathways primarily occurred during information pooling and integration phases. Quantitative results show that effective regulation predicts higher model - building performance, with sustained engagement emerging as the stable endpoint of productive collaboration. The findings provide a temporal, group- level account of how students collectively manage emotion to sustain effective problem solving.

title: A Preliminary Network Analysis of Theory and Methods in ICLS

abstract: This paper examines its thirty -year history as a complex adaptive system using network analysis to map the changing relationships among theories and methods from a small sample of 177 manually coded papers from the International Conference of the Learning Sciences. Findings suggest a possible shift from early separation between quantitative and qualitative paradigms toward a more complex multi -method theoretically diverse landscape. These preliminary findings offer a new perspective on the field's developing intellectual identity.

title: A Preliminary Study of Digital Tool Practices and Knowledge Building in Pre -service Teacher Learning within an Emerging Technology
citation: Yi-An Chen, Mei-Ju Chen, Yi-Ju Lin, Chao-Yu Guo, Huang-Yao Hong (2026). A Preliminary Study of Digital Tool Practices and Knowledge Building in Pre -service Teacher Learning within an Emerging Technology. Proceedings of ICLS 2026.
abstract: This study investigates how pre-service teachers engage in digital tool practices and develop knowledge -building competencies within an Emerging Technology Applications course at a national university in Taiwan. Guided by the frameworks of Knowledge Buildi ng (Scardamalia & Bereiter, 2010), reflective practice (Schön, 1983), and the Teaching Artist perspective (Eisner, 2002), the research examines how emerging technologies such as Padlet can transform teacher education into a creative and collaborative learn ing environment. Seventeen pre-service teachers participated in a three- phase design-based course: (1) personal expression and problem awareness, (2) collaborative feedback and campus inquiry, and (3) Sandbox co-creation of interactive materials integratin g SDGs or SEL. Data sources included the AI -TPACK questionnaire and Padlet discourse analyzed through theory- driven content analysis. Results show a developmental progression from individual tool use to community- oriented knowledge building, with Padlet evolving from a platform for expression to a site of co-construction and epistemic agency. The study contributes a replicable model demonstrating how digital design tasks can foster creativity, reflection, and sustained idea improvement in pre- service teacher education.

title: A Tale of Two Rivers: Pedagogical Implications Learned Through the Co- Design of an Environmental Engineering Curriculum
citation: Taryn Williams, Symone Gyles, Hosun Kang, Rossella Santagata, Yuxi Huang, Aakriti Bisht, Teresa Hachey, Jennifer Long, Erick Valdez, Sara Ludovise (2026). A Tale of Two Rivers: Pedagogical Implications Learned Through the Co- Design of an Environmental Engineering Curriculum. Proceedings of ICLS 2026.
abstract: As the impacts of climate change intensify, it is critical to support high school students in developing Critical Science Agency (CSA) and Systems Thinking (ST) to leverage science learning to address environmental concerns in their local communities and beyond. This study is part of a project involving a collaboration between university researchers, informal science educators, and high school students and teachers to codesign a place - and community- based environmental engineering curriculum. We explore pedagogical implications surfaced through the analysis of teacher and student codesign experiences and reflections that focus on community- embedded and relational environmental learning. Findings highlight the importance of physical presence to support critical and informed socio-ecological understanding of place.

title: A Teacher-in-the-Loop Multi-Agent Framework for Transparent Essay Scoring and Feedback
citation: Ali Keramati, Mark Warschauer (2026). A Teacher-in-the-Loop Multi-Agent Framework for Transparent Essay Scoring and Feedback. Proceedings of CSCL 2026.
abstract: We present MAESF, a multi-agent essay scoring and feedback, as a teacher-centered AI tool for scoring and feedback. The system distributes evaluation across specialized agents and enables educators to interactively query and refine rubric -aligned assessments. Evaluated on the ASAP dataset, MAESF outperforms single-agent baselines and approaches human inter- rater reliability. By combining transparent scoring with teacher-in-the-loop interaction, MAESF reframes automated assessment as a collaborative process that augments teacher capacity and supports more consistent, timely feedback.

title: A Transpositional Grammar Cyber-Social Study of Student–AI Relationships
citation: Christopher Hughes, Akash K. Saini (2026). A Transpositional Grammar Cyber-Social Study of Student–AI Relationships. Proceedings of CSCL 2026.
abstract: As AI -mediated feedback becomes embedded in higher education, understanding how learners construe relationships with AI and human reviewers becomes increasingly more important. This pilot applies Transpositional Grammar (TG) to student prompts, AI- generated images, and reflections in a cyber-social learning environment. Graduate students (n = 7; P300– P306) at a Midwestern U.S. research university contributed coursework artifacts coded collaboratively by a human researcher and GPT‑5, yielding Cohen’s κ = 0.761. TG analysis identifies five recurrent transpositions —expansion, visualization, reinterpretation, materialization, and affective deepening —and surfaces relational accountability as a new dimension of learner expectations. The full study (n = 35; P300–P334) will add a second human coder to triangulate interrater reliability and inform the design of affect- sensitive human–AI feedback ecosystems in graduate instruction.

title: A three-prong framework for designing theory-based math games
citation: Robin Sharma, Adam K. Dubé (2026). A three-prong framework for designing theory-based math games. Proceedings of ICLS 2026.
abstract: A common critique of ineffective learning games is their lack of theory-based design and integration of instructional features. While a few game-design frameworks have been proposed, they tend to take a limited approach. Some do not consider emotional aspects of games; others do not consider links between gameplay and learning. An approach that brings together the multiple aspects of educational game design is needed . This is important to build domain-specific thinking, build connections between gameplay and learning, and tap into the emotional and motivational aspects of games. This article describes an iterative approach to math game design by bringing together decades of previous research. It outlines how this approach is applied to create a game for secondary mathematics, specifically geometry. Progression of puzzles based on mathematical complexity, connections between learning objectives and gameplay, and inclusion of emotional elements are described. The challenges, opportunities, and outcomes of the approach are discussed. Gaps in math game design Interactive digital experiences like games can be useful tools for mathematics education as they can transform abstract mathematical concepts into concrete experiences (Potega vel Żabik et al., 2024). For example, games can simulate the abstract nature of mathematical concepts and provide low -stake and real -time interactive environments for mathematical problem solving (Hui & Mahmud, 2023; Klopfer & Thompson, 2020; Sharma et al., 2022). However, it is difficult to design games that incorporate such elements in a meaningful way to create an enjoyable and effective learning experience for adolescents (Vandercruysse et al., 2016). Despite their potential as engaging learning tools, research has shown that math games and interactive experiences have lacked theoretical foundations (Sharma & Dubé, 2024). More generally, researchers have regularly identified the need for theory -based development of educational games to make them more effective in achieving their intended learning goals (Dubé & Dubé, 2021; Vandercruysse et al., 2016). However, the challenge is to integrate learning into games while not taking away the “fun” (Garris et al. , 2002). From the learning perspective, ineffective educational games are criticized for lack of guiding theories and instructional features (Plass et al., 2015). From the fun perspective, ineffective games are criticized for their bad, unintuitive design, and a mismatch between learning goals and gameplay (Plass et al., 2015). It is important to bridge these gaps by grounding the design of math games in discipline and gameplay related theoretical frameworks. In their systematic review, Ke (2016) found that game-based learning (GBL) research has predominantly focused on evaluating the effectiveness of digital games. However, researchers should also elaborate and provide descriptions of theoretical foundations, design decisions, and rationales for their choice of game -interactions (Kiili & Lainema, 2008). In this article, we describe three dimensions to educational game design based on relevant theoretical frameworks. We present a three-prong approach to math game design. It builds on previous frameworks and suggests an iterative process of math game design that considers 1) mathematics instruction and thinking, 2) gameplay interactions tied with learning, and 3) the emotional aspects of games tied with learning. We describe this approach with an illustrative example of our process of creating GeometryBOX, a geometry game for adolescents. Three aspects of educational game design Discipline-specific theory Many researchers have called for educational games to be informed by learning theories guiding their designs (Plass et al., 2020). This can refer to a discipline-agnostic theory of learning (e.g., Constructivism). While such a theory can inform the game type and mode of learning, it does not address disciplinary needs. I t does not inform how the progression and order of in -game tasks align with the development of mathematical thinking. This requires a discipline-specific theory. A discipline -specific theory should be chosen to serve two purposes. First, it guides the in-game instruction and progression based on the requirements and the “ways of thinking” associated with the discipline (Honey & Hilton, 2011; Turkay et al., 2014). This can ensure that the game enables thinking processes in the player that are aligned with the requirements of the discipline (Mayer, 2020). Second, it informs all the subject matter -related aspects of the game, like operationalizing learning objectives for the in- game 61 problems. A discipline -specific theory informs how the in- game problems and gameplay intend to achieve the target learning outcomes (Plass et al., 2020). Gameplay-specific theory As opposed to the discipline specific theory that focusses on progression of in- game problems in line with the thinking process of the discipline, a gameplay specific theory informs the overall design of the game environment and specific player actions tied with the learning objectives. In their systematic review, Ke (2016) identified five themes and ways for integrating learning and playing in digital games. These provide a starting point for how learning goals could be mapped to the interactions offered by the game environment. The five themes are listed in Table 3 later in this article. However, it must be noted that these themes are not mutually exclusive, and one game can integrate learning opportunities in more than one way. The themes identified by Ke (2016) inform broad areas and approaches for integrating learning in games. In addition, it is also important to identify how learning content can be intrinsically embedded into the gameplay and mapped to player’s actions. This is needed to inform how all types of in-game player actions are associated with learning processes and to avoid unnecessary gameplay that can cause distractions and enhance extraneous load which can be detrimental to learning (Mayer & Moreno, 2003). Here, the Learning Mechanic – Game Mechanic (LM-GM) Framework (Arnab et al., 2015) can be a useful tool. It can be used to build a map of learning elements in a serious game with its mechanical/gameplay elements. Here, learning mechanics refers to the objectives, activities, and thinking processes focused on the context of learning. Game mechanics refers to the type of gameplay, game elements, and objects available to the player. This framework provides a starting point for designers to consider these mechanics and identify how gameplay and pedagogy are interrelated in their game. Educational game designers should carefully consider how each interaction a player makes in the game (game mechanic) is associated with the intended learning objective and processes (learning mechanic). This is useful to describe how the actions taken by the players in the games activate the thinking processes required for learning. Emotional design principles Games have the capability to induce achievement emotions that can support learning. Loderer and colleagues (2020) identified five emotional design principles to promote experiences and emotions that aid learning. Carefully considering emotional design principles to inform educational game design can help balance the “fun” and learning in games. Additionally, they can induce emotions conducive to learning like enjoyment and alleviation of boredom. Finally, emotional design principles in games can alleviate t he association of negative emotions, negative math attitudes, and math anxiety in children (Wen & Dubé, 2022; Young et al., 2012). The five principles are visual aesthetic design, musical score, game mechanics, narrative, and incentive system. Visual aesthetic design refers to the in -game visual elements that create engaging and immersive experiences. Musical scores in educational games refer to background tunes, sound effects, and audio feedback to enhance players’ experiences and learning. Game mechanics refer to the interactions and rules that drive the gameplay. Narrative refers to storylines and contextual problem solving that enhance engagement. Finally, the incentive system refers to the rewards and penalties to induce motivation during gameplay. Educational game designers should consider these five aspects at all stages of game development. When thoughtfully applied to its design, emotional design principles can make the game “fun” and “appealing” to the players while keeping intact the intended learning objectives (Mayer & Estrella, 2014). We propose an approach based on the three theoretical aspects of educational game design . Critically, all three should consistently inform design decisions across all aspects of the game (Figure 1). They are applied iteratively and inform the design process at all stages, which can include level design, characters, and in-game problems. Figure 1 Three-Prong Approach to Theory-Based Educational Game Design 62 GeometryBOX – a theory-based game for geometry “GeometryBOX” is designed for students in secondary grades, the game targets the topic of quadrilaterals. It specifically focusses on the following general learning outcomes: (a) to understand the relationships between properties of special quadrilaterals, and (b) to classify special quadrilaterals based on their properties. The game begins with the players assuming the role of a robot that is tasked to control a spacecraft while navigating outer space to collect as many stars as possible. The number of stars collected represents the overall game- score of the players. As they fly, they run out of resources which takes them to the internals of the ship. Here, they solve geometrical puzzles of increasing complexity to rebuild resources and return to the navigation gameplay. Players switch between these two primary types of gameplays as they increase their score (stars). The game finishes after they solve all geometrical puzzles. Discipline-specific theory in GeometryBOX As described previously, we aimed to identify a discipline -specific theoretical framework aligned with the intended learning objectives (geometry learning) and the target audience (adolescents). Additionally, it should inform the progression of in -game pro blems and enable the thinking processes needed to achieve learning objectives. To address these aspects, we used the Van Hiele Model (VHM) of geometric thinking (Hiele, 1999) as the guiding discipline specific theory for our game. It is a hierarchical framework establishing the existence of five different levels of geometric thinking of increasing complexity (Arnal -Bailera & Manero, 2024) . The increasing complexity of levels informed the increasing complexity of puzzles and specifically informed the “level design” of the game. Second, Hiele (1999) outlined the focus of the VHM on visual and non- verbal thinking and exploration which make it appropriate to inform the design of play- and game-based instruction. Finally, VHM is a topic-agnostic theoretical model. GeometryBOX targeted “classification of quadrilaterals”, a sub-topic in plane- geometry, generally included in middle and secondary geometry curriculum (Vízek et al., 2025) . The five levels of VHM are (a) visualization – referring to visual perception and recognition of mathematical objects; (b) analysis – referring to the ability to recognize and name properties of geometrical figures, (c) abstraction – referring to identification of properties and relationships between geometrical figures, (d) formal ded uction – referring to deduction of geometric proofs and understanding hierarchical nature of mathematical properties, and (e) rigor – referring to identification, comparison, and interrelation of different geometrical systems. VHM has previously been used to inform the design of several curricular and instructional materials for geometry (Senk et al., 2022). Table 2 shows how the definition of the VHM levels were operationalized for this topic (Crowley, 1987). Such operationalization is necessary to map how a theoretical model is applied to define the context of gameplay in association with the intended learn ing objectives. It breaks down the overarching aspects of the theoretical framework (VHM levels in this case) in relation to the target topic within the discipline. Table 2 VHM Levels Operationalized in GeometryBOX Van Hiele Level Key learning outcomes (Crowley, 1987) Learning outcomes operationalized for “classification of quadrilaterals” New game mechanics (1) Visualization Recognize and compare geometrical shapes. Compare, classify, and name geometrical shapes. Drag and drop geometrical shapes into respective bins. (20 puzzles) (2) Analysis Discern properties of geometrical figures. Progressively discover key differences between quadrilaterals of different types based on their properties. Drag and drop special quadrilaterals into respective bins. (27 puzzles) (3) Abstraction Establish interrelationship of properties between geometrical figures. Interrelate properties and relationships among different quadrilaterals. Target labels: see the label of the target bin (e.g., rectangles) to drag and drop shapes into. (20 puzzles) (4) Formal Deduction Deduce relationships and new properties based on axioms. Deduce properties of different quadrilaterals based on their diagonals. Slicing: “slice” a quadrilateral along one of its diagonals to get two triangles. (20 puzzles) 63 (5) Rigor Compare and operate within different geometrical systems. Make new shapes based on given conditions. Slicing: “slice” a quadrilateral along its altitudes to get two triangles and a rectangle; Combining shapes: certain triangles can be combined to obtain quadrilaterals. (20 puzzles) Gameplay specific theory in GeometryBOX Themes identified by Ke (2016) provide educational game designers with a tool to define how learning is integrated in the different aspects of the game. The example of GeometryBOX demonstrates integration of learning via all five themes in the context of mathematics. Table 3 describes how learning was integrated into the game based on Ke’s (2016) framework. Framing the in- game learning experiences in association with the five themes provides a clearer picture of how disciplinary learning objectives are integrated within the gameplay (See Figure 2 later in this article). Educational game designers should clearly identify how learning is integrated within their games. The themes identified here also inform the LM-GM map of the game. Table 3 Integrating Learning in GeometryBOX based on Ke (2016) Theme Description Integration in GeometryBOX game Learning as knowledge activation and acquisition Games with problem solving instances as contexts for retrieving previous knowledge and acquiring new knowledge. The game builds players’ knowledge of quadrilaterals, their properties, types, and relationship among properties through puzzles of increasing complexity. Each set of puzzles requires the players to retrieve knowledge acquired from the previous set. Learning via representation, simulation, or contextualization Game objects and rules embody the focus concepts and learning objectives. The game objects are tied to the narrative theme. The puzzles are contextualized in an overall narrative theme. The game objects (e.g., jewels) represent the mathematical objects (e.g., quadrilaterals) targeting the intended learning objectives. Learning via game mechanics and game world Game interactions and mechanics intrinsically represent the learning content. The game mechanics and interactions are centrally associated with the intended learning objectives. In- game puzzles require the players to sort and categorize geometrical shapes, this primary game mechanic mapped to the central learning objective: “classification of quadrilaterals”. Reflective and iterative learning moments in gameplay Learning happens via strategizing and reflective use of knowledge. Specific learning moments are repeated in gameplay. At least 20 puzzles are mapped to each learning outcome mapped to a Van Hiele Level (Table 2) providing iterative learning moments. Higher levels require strategizing, more complex thinking, and use of previous knowledge to solve puzzles. In-game learning supports Game provides cues, feedback, clear instructions, and in-game prompts. The game provides audio and textual feedback based on the players’ moves. It provides explicit hints and definitions associated with the learning objectives. An LM-GM map based on the framework by Arnab and colleagues (2015) is one of the most important parts of the educational game design process. It informs and presents a clear map of player interactions (game mechanics) and how they translate to learning rel ated actions (learning mechanics). All educational games should aim to create and describe the LM- GM map of their games. Table 4 shows the LM -GM map for GeometryBOX (also see Figure 2 later in this article). An LM-GM map lists the corresponding learning and game mechanics, the ways in which they are integrated, and “how” they are integrated. This framework provides a summary to educators and administrators and helps them make decisions about the suitability of the game for their use. When building the LM-GM map of the game, implementation and usage of learning mechanics and game mechanics is described in the context of game features. The exercise of creating an LM -GM map of the game is essential to reflect how different interactions and gameplay are linked to learning. Additionally, it is important to clearly communicate to users and other researchers the reasoning for their design decisions. 64 Table 4 LM-GM Map of GeometryBOX Game mechanic Learning mechanic Implementation via Usage Cut-scenes Story Motivation Feedback Narrative Game environment Levels 1) The overall guiding context and story of the game refer to the narrative theme. 2) The game has additional, story-related gameplay levels and cut- scenes beyond the geometrical puzzles that refer to the narrative theme. 3) Game scores (stars), health bars (shield and energy), and other visual elements (backdrop of game puzzles) also refer to the narrative theme. 4) The game provides textual and audio feedback based on the player actions associated with math learning and the narrative theme. Strategy/Planning Resource management Explore Discover Identify Hypothesize Plan Feedback In-game health bars Puzzles Levels 1) Puzzle solving encourages exploration and discovery by not giving any learning-outcome related instruction. 2) Exploration and discovery are encouraged by not penalizing initial incorrect moves. 3) Players hypothesize an approach to puzzle solving and plan their next move based on game feedback. 4) Complexity of puzzles and learning outcomes follows a hierarchical system where new knowledge is built on the previous. 5) In-game health bars represent the two types of resources available to the players. 6) Players need to identify the best strategy that optimizes resource usage when solving in-game puzzles. Rewards/Penalties Game turns Incentive Repetition In-game health bars Drag and drop action 1) Game turns refer to the action of dragging and dropping geometrical shapes into correct bins and locations. 2) Gameplay provides an incentive for taking the minimum number of turns when players solve a puzzle. 3) Incorrect moves beyond a threshold are penalized, correct moves are rewarded, and successful puzzle solving is rewarded. This is reflected by changes in available resources represented as health-bars. Feedback Motivation Feedback Game task Textual and visual prompts 1) Encouraging and motivational textual feedback prompts based on players’ in-game action (e.g., after a correct/incorrect move). 2) Learning outcome related textual feedback after successful completion of the game-task, i.e. solving a puzzle. Levels Analyze Simulation Repetition Reflection Puzzles Drag and drop action 1) Puzzles with game objects that simulate properties of geometrical objects. Shapes can be dragged-and-dropped on interactive elements to simulate their geometrical properties. 2) Correctly solving a puzzle requires analysis of shapes and application of knowledge. 3) Subsequent puzzles build on learning outcomes of previous puzzles. 4) Similar types of puzzles, referring to similar learning outcomes associated with VHM levels, are repeated several times. 5) Players can retry until the correct solution is found. However, too many incorrect moves deplete health and reduce progress encouraging reflection. Emotional design principles in GeometryBOX 65 Visual aesthetic design We used bright, warm, and contrasting colors in the visual design of the game. All the geometrical figures, that were the primary objects of gameplay, were bright purple in color to create a visually appealing interface (Wen & Dubé, 2023). The overall theme of “outer space” was consistently depicted through all the game objects. For example, the cursor was styled as a “crosshair”. Players solved geometrical puzzles to fix batteries and repair their ship. On the “progress map” screen of the game, the batteries were represented as “lightbulbs” that changed color from orange to green after successful completion of a puzzle. This aimed to create a sense of curiosity and break- down the overall game into smaller goals inducing a sense of achievement (Garg & Baroody, 2024). Musical score Audible feedback from a learning environment has the potential to enhance the perceived pleasantness of gameplay by extending the sensory experience (Nacke et al., 2010). A consistent, low, buzzing sound was used to convey the sound as their ship navigated outer space. Different types of audio feedback were used when players made correct/incorrect moves in the game, successfully completed a level, depleted their energy or shields, collected stars while navigating, an d shot enemy objects. Dynamic sounds along with encouraging phrases like “You’re good” (with a bright audio cue) after a correct move and “Try again” (with a dull audio cue) after an incorrect move were used to keep the players motivated during gameplay (Cayari, 2022). This way, the audio was also aligned with the game situation to induce immersion and emotional engagement (Andersen et al., 2021). Such acoustic characteristics were used in the game to draw attention to important content associated with learning (Collins, 2009; Plass et al., 2020). Game mechanics The central puzzle solving mechanic of the game was to “drag and drop” geometrical shapes into the correct bins to fix the batteries (Figure 2a, 2b). This built energy for the players’ ship to navigate and collect as many stars as possible. Sorting geometrical objects can engage students to build new knowledge based on their existing conceptions (Kobiela et al., 2018). It can help them identify and un derstand the properties of geometrical objects by noticing similarities and differences (Kobiela et al., 2018; Roth & Thom, 2009). Hence, sorting via “dragging and dropping” geometrical shapes into bins was built as the central game mechanic. Other game mechanics in the puzzles were primarily informed by the learning objectives at each level. New mechanics are introduced as players progress to puzzles at higher levels of the Van Hiele Model. They aim to sustain curiosity and enjoyment while preventing boredom and predictive gameplay (Loderer et al., 2020). They also create a sense of excitement as players progress in the game. For example, at puzzles from VHM level four, players are introduced to the “slicing” mechanic. They can break quadrilaterals into smaller diagonals by “slicing” them along a diagonal of their choice. Table 2 shows new mechanics introduced in puzzles at each new VHM level. In addition to inducing positive emotions that aid learning, the game mechanics are introduced in a structured order that is informed by the discipline-specific theory, the VHM model. This avoids a mismatch between progression of gameplay and learning which can enhance self -efficacy and reduce negative emotions such as frustration (Plass et al., 2012). This is associated with the recommendations of (Masek et al., 2017) where “fun” and “excitement” in the game are fundamentally grounded in the problem solving associated with learning. Narrative Narrative in educational games can provide a framework for structural representation of problems (Dickey, 2011). There can be many ways of including narrative in learning games. This is based on the genre of game and core game-mechanics (Ke, 2016) . Our game had a focus on mathematical learning outcomes. The core mechanic involved was “logic and thought during puzzle solving”. Additionally, it was categorized as a “casual puzzle” game as players solve geometrical puzzles to progress. In GeometryBOX, narrative was embedded via environmental storytelling and backdrop missions. Elements of the game environment focused on conveying the narrative theme of the game. Nomenclature for points, rewards, and penalties referred to the narrative theme. Additional gameplay puzzles for the game incentive system were created and were also situated in the overall narrative theme of the game (Figure 2c, 2d). In our game, narrative was integrated as a broadly defined goal with a background plot and adventure missions (Jenkins, 2002). An overarching narrative can create expectations about upcoming events and build suspense that sustains attention for learning (McNamara et al., 2010) . The narrative in GeometryBOX of “fixing batteries” to “repair the ship” and “navigate the outer space” was designed to contextualize learning and provide an overarching story connecting in- game progression, gameplay loop, rules, events, rewards, and penalties (Loderer et al., 2020) . Through all these aspects, narrative was tightly and meaningfully associated with gameplay and learning. It was not included as an afterthought where the story and narrative are only depicted through one aspect (e.g., cut scene and videos) and not tied to gameplay (Naul & Liu, 66 2020). On the contrary, the primary narrative related objective of “fixing batteries” was tied to the central learning objective of solving geometrical puzzles. Figure 2 Examples level screenshots from GeometryBOX Incentive system Rewards and penalties at the center of GBL can help keep the players motivated (Loderer et al., 2020). The incentive system in GeometryBOX is applied in three layers. First, every “game turn” of “dragging and dropping” an object costs a certain number of resources. In this way, players are nudged towards solving the puzzles in minimum possible moves to pres erve the available resources. Hence, they are incentivized for adopting mathematical strategies and discourage “trial and error” based strategy. Second, when players deplete all their resources by making too many incorrect moves, they need to replenish it by completing another game level where they “shoot the debris to clear the boosters” (Figure 2d). This resets their available resources to 100%. This incentive system of managing resources and performance-based progress is dependent on individual learning and gameplay strategy. It aims to increase perceived autonomy and learner control and induce positive achievement emotions (McNamara et al., 2010). The third layer of incentive system is based on collecting “stars” to increase overall points. This layer in tends to enhance the value of learning through “internal compensation”, i.e. achievements in the game (Loderer et al., 2020). After players solve enough puzzles to bring their available resources above a certain threshold, new gameplay is unlocked in which the player controls their spaceship and steers it through an “asteroid field in outer space”. This three -layered, cyclic incentive system in GeometryBOX is intended to create positive achievement emotion of anticipation through feedback, novelty, and repe tition (Pekrun et al., 2014). It also aims to promote optimized gameplay linked with learning as thoughtful, strategized, and mathematical gameplay is rewarded. In sum, GeometryBOX is designed for adolescents to understand the properties and relationships between special quadrilaterals. It is tightly aligned with the learning objectives associated with this topic. This aspect was primarily informed by the VHM, the discipline-specific theory guiding its design. The gameplay and learning were integrated based on the five themes identified by Ke (2016) and are described via its LM-GM map. Emotional design principles were applied to all five features of the game to create a positive and enjoyable learning experience for the players. Discussion This article suggests a three -prong approach to educational game design with an elaborate example of a math game. Educational game designers should follow an iterative process of applying this approach to their design. They should bring these three theoretical approaches together by going beyond previous approaches to educational 67 game design that only consider these aspects independently. In their review of existing educational game design frameworks, Sasupilli and colleagues (2019) identified six prevalent game design models. However, none of them focused on domain specific, play specific, and emotion specific theoretical foundations simultaneously. They were limited to either one or only two of these aspects. For example, the experiential gaming model (Kiili, 2005) does not consider blending learning through game mechanics. In the context of mathematics education, the application of a theoretical framework of math instruction is critical to promote students’ domain -specific mental models for learning (Pirnay -Dummer et al., 2012). This factor becomes much more critical in the context of math as it relies on students’ development of mental models of mathematical objects, their properties, and their relationships (G arg et al., 2025 ; Prayekti et al., 2020). Additionally, the use of Ke’s (2016) framework is needed to address the “what, how, where, and when learning is embedded” in games. This framework helps game designers answer broader questions about leaning in games. It informs design decisions like choice of game genre (simulation versus puzzle), absence or presence of narrative, narrative design (environmental backdrop versus roleplay), representation of learning content (content as game objects versus simulation of concepts), frequency of learning moments in games (exploration and discovery versus immediate feedback), and presence or absence of in-game learning supports. Further, at a finer level, the LM-GM framework (Arnab et al., 2015) helps designers address how all game features (game mechanics) are linked to learning mechanics. Creating an LM-GM map of the game during its design process is crucial to establish granular relationships between pedagogy and gameplay. Finally, to leverage the potential of games to induce emotional experiences for learning, the application of emotional design principles is essential. This can ensure a balance between fun and learning by fostering positive emotions (Byun & Joung, 2018). Specifically for mathematics, enhancing the overall learning experience can be transformative to address concerns with the negative perception of math as being too challenging and uninspiring (Wen & Dubé, 2023). Careful integration of emotional design principles that meaningfully and systematically induce enjoyment, anticipation, and excitement (Putwain et al., 2018) can counter negative impressions of math like fear and anxiety (Budhathoki et al., 2022). Navigating challenges While there are theoretical benefits of applying the three- prong framework to educational games, it also comes with its own challenges and opportunities. It is possible that there is overlap, friction, and conflict when certain game elements are informed by two approaches. The design process for GeometryBOX serves as an example to illustrate how such challenges can be overcome. This is mainly exhibited by two elements: game mechanics and narrative. We describe how all game mechanics were linked to learning via the LM-GM map of the game. The LM-GM map describes the way in which mechanics were implemented and their link with learning processes. In addition, a range of game mechanics were built to create anticipation and excitement as an outcome of the emotional design principles. Further, the addition of new mechanics to create anticipation and excitement was based on the increasing complexity of the discipline -specific VHM model. This way, the design of game mechanics was grounded in all three frameworks that each supported learning through different dimensions. Similarly, learning was integrated through an implicit narrative in the game via environmental storytelling, backdrop, textual and visual references to narrative theme. This was based on Ke’s (2016) framework. Narrative can be beneficial for math learning by providing learners with a framework for representation of problems (Irmayanti et al., 2024; Junkin, 2019). Here, narrative was not included as explicit framing but, rather, the action of solving geometry puzzles to achieve learning outcomes was implicitly linked to the game narrative (solving puzzles = fixing “batteries” = repairing “ship”). Moreover, narrative served as a tool to create an immersive and enjoyable learning experience based on the emotional design principles. This demonstrates how the inclusion of narrative was also informed by two distinct frameworks. Yet, it aimed to avoid contradictory and conflicting experiences. In this case, grounding the narrative in multiple theoretical argument s is likely to strengthen its effects on learning rather than weakening it. Conclusion The GeometryBOX game described in this article is an example of applying distinct but relevant theoretical frameworks of educational game design to create a geometry game. It bridges the gaps between cognitive and domain-specific, gameplay-specific, and emotional foundations of game-based learning. Thoughtful and implicit design of game features tightly tied to learning objectives have the potential to result in positive learning outcomes and make learning an enjoyable experience. We aim to conduct evidence -based, experimental studies on the effectiveness of GeometryBOX on geometrical understanding of adolescents . Game designers should consider this approach to create educational games that are not only grounded in theories of learning and instruction but also harness the power of play in a holistic way. 68 References Andersen, F., Danny, King, C. title: A “Co-Design Intervention” with AI analytics to Support the Academically Productive Talk of Title 1 School Math Tutors and their Students: A Comparative Interrupted Time Series Analysis
citation: Amirpasha Zandieh, Jeffrey Bush Tayne, Chelsea Brown, Jennifer Jacobs, Sandra Sawaya (2026). A “Co-Design Intervention” with AI analytics to Support the Academically Productive Talk of Title 1 School Math Tutors and their Students: A Comparative Interrupted Time Series Analysis. Proceedings of ICLS 2026.
abstract: This study examines whether a co- design-based professional learning intervention for tutors, supported by an AI feedback tool, influenced students’ Academically Productive Talk (APT) within a high-dosage algebra tutoring program in Title 1 schools in an urban U.S. school district. Using a comparative interrupted time series (CITS) design, we analyzed 9,037 tutoring sessions over the 42 weeks of one academic year, comparing tutors who participated in a nine - week co-design process with those who did not. Tuto rs in the intervention co -designed an AI interface called the “Talk Trees”, visualizing student talk patterns to guide student reflection on collaborative discourse. Results show short -term, positive shifts in students’ relating to academic ideas of their peers following the intervention, with modest, non- significant gains in instances of students making claims and providing reasoning. These findings highlight co- design’s potential to foster dialogic pedagogy in the context of boundary-crossing professional learning. They also demonstrate how CITS methods can evaluate AI-mediated interventions in authentic educational contexts.

title: AI Competence in STEM Education: An Exploratory Study of STEM Educators’ Confidence, Knowledge, and Pedagogical Practices
citation: Hulya Avci (2026). AI Competence in STEM Education: An Exploratory Study of STEM Educators’ Confidence, Knowledge, and Pedagogical Practices. Proceedings of ICLS 2026.
abstract: This exploratory study examines STEM educators’ perceptions of their confidence, knowledge, and use of artificial intelligence (AI) technologies, as well as their views on the impact of AI on teaching and learning. Using a mixed- methods survey design, data were analyzed through descriptive statistics and thematic analysis. Findings revealed substantial variation in perceived AI knowledge, confidence, and pedagogical practices. Participants described developing AI competence through self-directed learning and professional networks, with limited access to structured training. Reported AI applications in teaching included lesson planning, feedback generation, and student projects, with practices var ying depending on purpose, familiarity, and access. While educators recognized AI benefits, such as increased efficiency and scaffolds for student learning, they also expressed concerns related to academic integrity, overreliance, and equity. These findings offer preliminary insights to inform future large-scale studies on ethical and equitable AI integration strategies responsive to disciplinary practices across STEM disciplines.

title: AI Literacy in CS Education
citation: Yob Ha, Chih-Pu Dai (2026). AI Literacy in CS Education. Proceedings of ICLS 2026.
abstract: This study systematically reviews 27 peer -reviewed studies on AI literacy in computer science (CS) education, including five broader STEM studies as comparative cases . Using PRISMA, it synthesizes evidence across conceptual, ethical, and pedagogical dimensions. Results show advances in data competencies but persistent challenges in ethics integration, assessment, and teacher preparation. The study highlights both STEM -wide trends and CS-specific needs, offering actionable guidance for designing coherent and sustainable AI literacy curricula.

title: AI Tools in Arts Learning: A Scoping Review
citation: Jaycee Sansom, Safinah Ali (2026). AI Tools in Arts Learning: A Scoping Review. Proceedings of CSCL 2026.
abstract: With the proliferation of Artificial Intelligence (AI) tools in art making, AI knowledge and skills have made their way to arts learning. However, an assessment of the current state of AI tools in arts learning is lacking. This study used scoping review methodology to identify current research trends in AI applications in arts learning, and what gaps exist for future research. 58 papers were reviewed revealing four trends and five gaps and opportunities.

title: AI agents as a Refinement Tool for Operationalizing Coding Process in the Context of Textbook Analysis
citation: Boram Lee, Seyedehkhadijeh Azimi (2026). AI agents as a Refinement Tool for Operationalizing Coding Process in the Context of Textbook Analysis. Proceedings of ICLS 2026.
abstract: Qualitative research often employs coding to analyze complex data, yet even with codebooks, the operational criteria guiding coders’ decisions frequently remain implicit. This gap limits transparency and comparability across studies. We explore how an AI agent (ChatGPT-5) can function as a refinement tool to surface and formalize tacit reasoning in coding. Using textbook analysis as a case, we applied the Cognitive Demand Level (CDL) framework to 47 fraction- related problems from Grade 3 mathematics textbooks in Iran and Korea. Through iterative engagement, ChatGPT -5’s discrepant coding prompted us to articulate, refine, and document operational criteria, evolving from an intuitive flowchart to a detailed criteria table. This process transformed implicit reasoning into explicit decision rules that can be scrutinized and tested by others. title: AI as a Collaborative Partner: EMPA’s Role in Supporting Reflective Teamwork Learning
citation: Aparajita Jaiswal, Ashish Ashish (2026). AI as a Collaborative Partner: EMPA’s Role in Supporting Reflective Teamwork Learning. Proceedings of CSCL 2026.
abstract: Teamwork requires students to reflect on their practices, yet individualized mentoring is often limited. While AI tutoring systems increasingly support learning, most position AI as external evaluator rather than collaborative partner. We present EMPA, an AI - based collaborative partner that scaffolds teamwork learning through case studies, activities, and videos. Grounded in Schön’s reflection -in-action and reflection -on-action, EMPA encourages students to adapt strategies during tasks and analyze experiences afterwards. Students engage with scenarios and activities while EMPA prompts real -time reflection, then receive personalized summaries and complete surveys that consolidate learning. Early deployment with undergraduates shows EMPA’s potential to help learners examine assumptions, recognize cultural dynamics, and develop strategies for improving collaboration. This study operationalizes Schön’s framework via AI-supported mentoring, positioning AI as a reflective partner to scale practice and strengthen teamwork.

title: AI-Enhanced Sociocultural, Multimodal Approaches for Equitable Collaborative Learning: Learning, Power, and Multimodality

abstract: My research lies at the intersection of the learning sciences, learning analytics, and Science, Technology, Engineering and Mathematics education, and centers on making collaborative learning more equitable for K–12 learners, particularly multilingual, multicultural, and marginalized youth. Across three interconnected lines of inquiry, I position myself as a scholar who bridges the learning sciences and learning analytics, advancing theoretically grounded, situated, and equity-oriented approaches to illuminate the complexity of collaborative learning at multiple scales.

title: AI-Feedback System: Integrating Human-in-the-Loop for Customized Support
citation: Namsoo Shin, Cory Miller, Xunlei Qian, Joe Krajcik, Yue Xing (2026). AI-Feedback System: Integrating Human-in-the-Loop for Customized Support. Proceedings of ICLS 2026.
abstract: This study presents an iterative human- AI collaboration design process for developing an AI -Feedback system aligned with learning theories, providing timely, customized feedback to support teachers and students in developing usable knowledge. The process involved collaboration among teachers, content experts, and learning scientists to refine rubrics and validate AI models for analyzing elementary students’ written responses on complex science tasks—often vague or inconsistent —to identify weaknesses and uncertainty in students’ understanding. Using a multi -agent human-in-the-loop system, we improved analytical accuracy, quantified uncertainty, and generated analytical rationales to guide customized feedback. Analyses of 90 student responses demonstrates an overall accuracy 88%, showing that integrating Generative AI with continuous expert guidance can provide reliable and meaningful feedback, even for lower elementary student writing.

title: AI-Scaffolded Summarization in STEM: How do Students Differ in Writing and Revision?
citation: Hyunkyu Han, Seora Kim, Mohamed Shameer Abdeen, Min Kyu Kim (2026). AI-Scaffolded Summarization in STEM: How do Students Differ in Writing and Revision?. Proceedings of ICLS 2026.
abstract: Summarization is a key learning strategy in undergraduate STEM, yet students often struggle without timely, effective feedback. This study investigates how a n AI-scaffolded feedback system (SMART) relates to students’ revision behaviors and how these patterns vary across diverse student backgrounds. We analyzed 1,081 summary revisions from 49 undergraduates in an introductory physics course using a suite of mixed-effects models. Results show that adding concepts and words while maintaining semantic coherence predicted stronger concept learning, whereas excessive deletion corresponded to weaker outcomes. Revision patterns differed meaningfully by gender, race/ethnicity, and academic level, suggesting that AI-scaffolded feedback needs to be tailored to support diverse learners toward productive revision strategies.

title: AI/ML Education in Motion: Embodied Machine Learning with Wearable Technology in Informal Contexts
citation: Manav Sharma, Ji Shen (2026). AI/ML Education in Motion: Embodied Machine Learning with Wearable Technology in Informal Contexts. Proceedings of ICLS 2026.
abstract: Systematic reviews on the application of AI technologies in STEM Education recommend the use of age -appropriate AI/ML tools in primary and secondary school settings, in contexts that appeal to students’ interests. In this pilot we incorporate a new modality (body movement) and tool (BBC micro:bit) into an AI/ML unit for young learners to understand how they engage with machine learning concepts. Students articulated novel uses for ML tools, drew connections to other practices, demonstrated metacognitive awareness, and described their roles as designers. These findings highlight the value of scaffolded, collaborative, embodied learning designs in supporting emerging AI literacy.

title: Adaptive Equity-Oriented Pedagogy Predicts Student Achievement in Higher Education: Evidence from a Multi-Site Study
citation: Andrew Estrada Phuong, Fan Huang, Judy Nguyen, Carolyn Huie Hofstetter, Bowen Wang- Kildegaard, Fabrizio D. Mejia, Christopher T. Hunn, Stanley M. Lo (2026). Adaptive Equity-Oriented Pedagogy Predicts Student Achievement in Higher Education: Evidence from a Multi-Site Study. Proceedings of ICLS 2026.
abstract: This study investigates whether equity- oriented teaching competencies predict college students’ success. In pedagogy courses, 143 graduate and undergraduate student instructors (hereafter “instructors”) completed the Adaptive Equity- Oriented Pedagogy (AEP) Competency assessment after teaching lessons. This portfolio -based assessment asked instructors to document observable AEP competencies and evaluated how instructors planned, taught, reflected, and adapted to address students’ equity barriers. This previ ously validated AEP competency assessment has demonstrated strong reliability, exhibits no gender bias, and correlates with researchers’ independent review of instructors’ teaching methods and materials. At two R1 institutions, multilevel regression modeling suggests that higher AEP competency scores significantly predicted greater student achievement in 14+ STEM and Social Science courses, controlling for instructors’ course, class size, teaching experience, minoritized status, and gender. Furthermore, addressing the pernicious belief that equity undermines rigor in curriculum, this study provides evidence suggesting that centering equity through AEP can improve instructor and student success.
